title: The Fast of Esther (Esther 4:16)
hook: a fast the day before Purim, for Esther's three days of fasting

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tu BiShvat's planting, and Choni's carob tree. Your line was plant something. Did you start something someone else will enjoy? Today we move to late winter, and the road to Purim. Day six hundred seventy-two.

A young woman is standing outside a door. Behind it sits the king of Persia, who also happens to be her husband. There's a law: anyone who walks into the king's inner court without being called is put to death, unless the king holds out his golden scepter. She hasn't been called in thirty days. And her people, the Jews of the Persian empire, have a date set for their destruction. Her cousin Mordecai has just told her that if she stays silent, she may not escape either. She doesn't go in yet. First, she sends back a message.
screen: `A DOOR SHE CAN'T WALK THROUGH.` → `NOT CALLED IN THIRTY DAYS.` → `FIRST, A MESSAGE.`

segments.voice: Esther's message is in chapter four. She asks Mordecai to gather all the Jews of Shushan and fast for her: no food, no drink, for three days, night and day. She and her maids will fast too. Then she'll go in to the king, against the law. And her last words, in the old Jewish translation: "and if I perish, I perish." The line is very quiet. No speech about courage. Just a decision, and a fast to get ready for it. Now, the Fast of Esther as people keep it today falls on the thirteenth of Adar, the day before Purim. But the book never dates Esther's own three-day fast, and its timeline leads tradition to place it in the spring month of Nisan, almost a year earlier. So why the thirteenth of Adar? The thirteenth was the day set for the attack, and the day the Jews had to defend themselves. Later authorities explain that people fasted and prayed on that day of battle, as they had with Esther. The book itself, near its end, mentions fasts and cries as part of what the Jews took on. The fast is first described as a custom after the Talmud's time, and it's one of the minor fasts: dawn to nightfall, and anyone ill, pregnant or nursing is usually excused. Health comes first. If Purim falls on a Sunday, the fast moves back to Thursday, so it doesn't land on Shabbat. In the afternoon, there's a custom of giving coins to charity, recalling the half-shekel. And at nightfall, the fast breaks straight into Purim: the scroll is read, and the feast begins. Hunger first. Then joy.
screen: `FAST FOR ME, THREE DAYS.` · `IF I PERISH, I PERISH.` · `WHY THE THIRTEENTH OF ADAR?` · `DAWN TO NIGHTFALL, THEN PURIM.` · then, large: `BEFORE THE FEAST, A FAST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go without one thing. Not to suffer. To get ready. Before the bell, choose one small thing to skip today: a snack, a scroll through your phone, your second coffee, a complaint you usually make. Picture the moment you'll want it, and what you'll do instead. Then breathe, and think of one hard thing ahead of you, a conversation, a decision, a door you'll have to walk through. Let the small fast be your preparation. The bell holds the time.
Mordecai, Esther's cousin, who warned her that silence wouldn't save her, and whose message led to the fast before she risked her life before the king.

Your line: before the feast, a fast. A week of a little that lasts, a light in the window, a rock of ages, unknown dates, fruit, planting, and now a fast. Today, skip your one thing, and let it get you ready. Day six hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: On the Fast of Esther, the thirteenth of Adar, observant Jews fast from dawn until nightfall, often give charity in the afternoon in memory of the half-shekel, and break the fast after hearing the Megillah read on Purim night.

notes: Added 2026-10-06 from the five-year map (standing rule: every fast-day lesson carries the health line; never present fasting as required at risk to health): one sentence that health and life come first. Tisha B'Av: the ill and anyone at risk eat; others ask a doctor and a rabbi (OC 554:5-6). Confirm with the Keeper.
